meta.blurb: Every midnight, Iris climbs her lighthouse to check a lamp that has never gone dark. Then an engineer arrives on the last ferry, sent to decide whether it should be switched off for good. He is hiding something about that light.
meta.bible: Iris Calloway: twenty-eight, runs the Lighthouse Inn at Gull Point, brave and stubborn; her father Tom Calloway was the last keeper and died four winters ago; her mother left when she was small. Elias Thorne: thirty-one, an engineer sent by the Harbour Authority to examine the lighthouse; as a boy of ten he was saved on a stormy ferry crossing by the light, but he keeps this secret until the end. Abel Hurst: eighty years old, a retired keeper who lives at the inn, plays the accordion and tells stories. Rosa Tamm: the inn's cook, round, practical and wise. Bosun: the inn's old brown dog. Mr Dray: Fenwick Dray, a senior official of the Harbour Authority, in favour of closing the old lamp. Captain Mara Quill: master of the ferry Kittiwake, which crosses between Harrow Island and the mainland. The Lighthouse Inn: the stone inn at the foot of the tower, built for keepers' families, with a warm kitchen and a stove. Gull Point: the headland on Harrow Island where the inn and the tower stand. Harrow Bay: the water between the island and the mainland. Harrow Island: a windy island in the north. The old lamp: a great lamp turned by clockwork weights and a gear; the machine beacon: an electric light that runs by itself and goes dark if the power fails. The logbook: the keeper's book in which Tom wrote every night. The Harbour Authority: the body that runs the harbour and its lights. The light has not been dark for more than a hundred years. Voice and tone: romantic, atmospheric and warm, with storms outside and firelight inside; a chaste romance; danger is described plainly and without gore; the ending is happy and earned.

A1A2: Iris climbed the lighthouse stairs at midnight, as her father always did.
A stranger called Elias came on the last ferry and asked for a room.
At supper Rosa served hot soup, and Bosun the dog sat by Elias.
Elias said he was there to look at the lighthouse for the Harbour Authority.
Old Abel said the light had never gone out in over a hundred years.
At midnight Elias followed Iris up the tower and looked out at the sea.
Iris said her father taught her about the lamp before he died.
Next day Elias looked at the machine and found a small crack.
Iris showed Elias the cliff path and the seals sleeping on the rocks.
When the boiler broke in the cold, Elias fixed it, and Iris thanked him.
That evening Abel played a happy song, and Iris and Elias danced.
A letter came from Mr Dray saying the old light might be closed.
Iris was angry, but Elias promised to write a fair report.
Elias worked at night in the tower, and Iris brought him tea.
Abel told Elias that Iris's father wrote in a big book every night.
Iris showed Elias the old book, full of her father's careful words.
Elias read about one stormy night long ago, and he knew that night.
On the longest night the islanders came to the inn, and Elias hung the lanterns.
It snowed, and Iris and Elias walked to the tower together.
At the top of the tower at midnight, they kissed.
The winter days were happy, with long walks, laughter and Bosun running ahead.
Elias began to write his report, but he did not know what to say.
Rosa told Elias to tell Iris the truth about the stormy night.
Mr Dray came to the inn with a plan for a machine light only.
Iris said no, but Mr Dray said the engineer's report would decide.
Iris saw one line in the report: the old lamp is not safe.
Iris said Elias had come to close her light, and she would not listen.
Elias packed his bag, and Abel told Iris she was being proud.
Elias left on the ferry in the grey morning and left a letter.
Iris was alone, and Bosun waited at the door every evening.
At midnight Iris climbed alone, and the old lamp made a sad noise.
Rosa told Iris to open the letter, and at last she did.
Inside was Elias's report, and it said to mend the lamp and keep it.
Iris understood, and she felt sorry, so she wrote him a long letter.
A storm warning came, and Abel said he could feel it in his knees.
At dusk the power failed, and the machine light went out across the bay.
On the radio they heard that the ferry was lost in the storm.
The old lamp could only turn by hand now, so Iris and Abel climbed up.
The islanders came and took turns at the handle all through the night.
On the ferry, Elias held the new part and saw the light turn.
The captain followed the light past the rocks and reached the harbour at dawn.
People cheered, and Mr Dray, who was on the ferry, said nothing.
Elias ran up the cliff path with the new part in his arms.
At the tower door, they said sorry, and he told her about the boy.
Mr Dray came up and said he had seen the light, and it must stay.
The Harbour Authority agreed to repair the lamp and keep the tower open.
In spring Elias put the new part in, and the lamp turned smoothly.
One midnight in the tower, Elias asked Iris to marry him, and she said yes.
In summer they married on the cliff, and Abel played music all day.
A year later, they climbed the tower together at midnight, and a ship sailed safely past.
B1B2: Every night at midnight, Iris Calloway climbs the spiral stairs of the old lighthouse, a lantern swinging in her hand. A machine now runs the main light, but she checks the old lamp anyway, because her father always did.
The last ferry of the day lands in heavy rain, and a tall stranger in a wet coat walks up to the Lighthouse Inn. He gives his name as Elias Thorne and asks if there is a room for the whole winter.
At supper, Rosa the cook serves a thick soup, and old Abel tells a story that makes even the dog look up. Bosun, who usually ignores strangers, lies down on Elias's boots and refuses to move.

Over the second bowl, Elias explains that he is an engineer sent by the Harbour Authority to examine the lighthouse. Iris puts down her spoon and says nothing, but Rosa sees the worry that crosses her face.

Abel leans back by the stove and tells Elias that the inn was built for the keepers' families long ago. In more than a hundred years, he says proudly, the light on Gull Point has never once been dark.

At midnight Elias is waiting at the foot of the tower, and Iris, a little annoyed, lets him climb with her. At the top the great lamp stands in its glass room, and below it the black sea rolls all the way to the sky.

Iris tells him that her father, Tom, was the last keeper and taught her everything about the lamp. He died four winters ago, and since then she has kept the old lamp ready for the stormy nights when the machine is not enough.

The next morning Elias lies on the tower floor with a torch, looking at the gears that turn the lamp. He finds a hairline crack in one of them, and because he is not yet sure what it means, he keeps it to himself.

Iris takes him for a walk along the cliff path, where the wind is wild and the grass is silver with frost. Below them, a family of seals lies on the rocks like grey sacks, and Elias laughs for the first time since he arrived.

One freezing night the inn's boiler breaks down, and the guests are huddled in blankets by the stove. Elias goes into the cellar with a toolbox and Iris holds the lamp, and an hour later the pipes are warm again.

After supper Abel brings out his accordion and plays a slow, sweet tune from his youth. Before she can think about it, Iris finds herself dancing across the kitchen floor with Elias, while Rosa and the dog watch.

A letter arrives from Mr Dray of the Harbour Authority, and Iris reads it twice at the kitchen table. It says that the Authority will decide after the winter whether the old lamp should be switched off for good.

Iris realises that Elias's report will help to decide the old lamp's future, and she tells him angrily that he should have said so earlier. He promises to be fair, and after a cold, silent walk to the cliff edge, they make peace.

In the evenings Elias works in the tower, and Iris climbs up with tea and sits beside him among the gears. He tells her that his father was often away at sea, and she tells him that her mother left when she was small.

Abel hands Elias a worn leather book beside the fire and says that Tom Calloway wrote in it every single night. He adds that Tom turned down every offer to sell the inn, because he believed the light belonged to the sea.

Iris takes the logbook from its shelf and shows Elias her father's careful handwriting by candlelight. Every page records the weather, the ships and the hours of the lamp, and some of the entries describe terrible storms.

Turning the pages, Elias stops at a night in winter more than twenty years ago, when a ferry was lost in a gale. His heart pounds, because he knows that night better than anyone, but he closes the book and says nothing.

At midwinter the islanders gather at the inn for the lantern evening, which has been held for as long as anyone remembers. Elias climbs a ladder to hang the lanterns along the porch, and the whole building glows against the dark.

That night snow begins to fall, thick and silent, and Iris takes Elias's arm as they walk towards the tower. The headland has vanished under white, and the sea beyond it makes only a soft, distant sound.
At the top of the tower the great lamp turns slowly, and its beam moves across the whirling snow. Iris and Elias stand close together, and at the stroke of midnight, he kisses her.

The following weeks are the happiest of the winter, with long walks over the frozen headland and picnics in sheltered corners. Bosun runs ahead barking at the seals, and Iris finds that she laughs more than she has in years.

Elias begins to write his report at last, but the words will not come, because the truth is more complicated than any form allows. He thinks of the cracked gear, of the old lamp and of the woman he has come to love.

Rosa, kneading dough in the kitchen, tells him firmly that he must tell Iris about the night on the ferry. He says that he will, once the report is finished, and she shakes flour from her hands and gives him a doubtful look.

One grey morning Mr Dray arrives at the inn in a long dark coat, with an official plan under his arm. He wants to close the old lamp, leave the machine light to do the work, and buy the inn from Iris for a generous price.

Iris stands in front of her door with her arms folded and tells him that the inn is not for sale. Mr Dray replies politely that the engineer's report will settle everything, and that he expects it within the week.

That night Iris finds the draft report lying on the kitchen table and cannot help reading a line at the bottom. It says that the old lamp is unsafe to run and should be shut at once, and she feels the floor tip beneath her.

She tells Elias in a shaking voice that he came to close her light and that everything between them was a lie. He tries to explain about the cracked gear, but she is too hurt to listen, and she points to the door.
Elias packs his bag in silence while Abel stands in the hall and tells Iris that she is being proud and foolish. She says she is not listening, and goes to bed without saying goodnight.
At dawn Elias walks down to the quay and boards the ferry without looking back. On the hall table he has left a thick envelope, with Iris's name on it, and Rosa quietly puts it in a drawer.
The inn feels cold and empty without him, and Bosun sits by the door each evening staring down the road. Iris keeps busy with the guests and the cooking, but her smile never quite reaches her eyes.

At midnight she climbs the tower alone, and the old lamp turns with a long, sad groan that she has not heard before. She lays her hand against the cold metal and wonders if her father would have known what to do.
Rosa puts the envelope on the table one morning and tells Iris that no one can be proud for ever. After a long minute, Iris picks it up and opens it with fingers that are not quite steady.
Inside are the full pages of Elias's report, and she reads them slowly in the grey light. He recommends that the old lamp be repaired with a new gear and kept alive for the sake of the sailors.

At the back of the report is a letter in which Elias explains that he never meant to close the light. Iris puts her face in her hands, then takes a pen and writes him a long and honest letter of apology.

A storm warning comes over the radio, and Abel rubs his knees and says that he can feel something terrible on its way. The islanders tie down their boats, close their shutters, and gather what they need for a long night.
At dusk the wind rises to a scream, and the power fails across the island. The machine beacon goes dark, and the whole of Harrow Bay, from the cliffs to the mainland, lies in blackness.

Over the crackling radio, Iris hears Captain Quill report that the ferry Kittiwake is somewhere in the bay without a light to steer by. The sea is huge, and the rocks around Gull Point are the most dangerous on the coast.
Iris and Abel run up the tower stairs and find the old lamp's cracked gear jammed fast. If the light is to turn tonight, someone will have to turn it by hand, using the great iron crank.

One by one the islanders climb the tower, take their turn at the handle and pass it on when their arms ache. Rosa brings tea and soup, Bosun lies at the top of the stairs, and the light keeps on sweeping the dark water.

On the pitching ferry, Elias holds a heavy parcel with the new gear inside and peers through the spray. Suddenly the old light sweeps across the waves, and he remembers a frightened boy who once saw it from a boat.

Captain Quill steers by the beam, counting the seconds between its sweeps and threading the ferry between the rocks. At last the dark shape of the harbour wall rises out of the dawn, and everyone on board begins to breathe again.
A crowd has gathered on the quay, and a great cheer goes up as the ferry's lines are thrown ashore. Mr Dray, who is among the passengers, steps off pale and silent and stares up at the headland.
Elias grabs the parcel and begins to run, up the steep path along the cliff and through the cold grey light. His legs burn and his lungs ache, but he does not stop until he reaches the tower door.

Iris is standing there with a face grey from the long night, and for a moment neither of them speaks. Then they both say sorry, and Elias tells her that he was the boy in her father's logbook, the one the light saved.
Mr Dray climbs slowly up the cliff, enters the lantern room, and takes off his hat. He tells them quietly that he was on the ferry and that he saw the light, and that it must never be put out.
Within the week the Harbour Authority agrees to pay for the repair of the old lamp. The tower will become a heritage light, and the Lighthouse Inn will be its keepers' lodge, with Iris in charge.
Spring arrives, and Elias fits the new gear with Iris holding the lantern steady beside him. When the lamp turns again, it moves smoothly and silently, with a soft, steady rhythm like a heartbeat.

One night at midnight, standing beside the great lamp, Elias takes a small ring from his pocket and asks Iris to marry him. She says yes before he has finished speaking, and the beam sweeps over the sea as if to applaud.

In the summer they are married on the cliff, with the sea shining below and the whole island in their best clothes. Abel plays the accordion until the stars come out, and Bosun, who carries the rings in a small box, behaves perfectly.

A year later, at the stroke of midnight, Iris and Elias climb the tower stairs together with a lantern. Out on the dark water a ship passes safely beneath the turning light, and neither of them has any wish to be anywhere else.
C1C2: Every night at midnight, whatever the weather, Iris Calloway climbed the spiral staircase of the old lighthouse on Gull Point, her lantern swinging against the curved walls. A modern beacon now ran the main light by itself, but she inspected the old lamp each night all the same, partly from habit and partly because her father had done so for forty winters. In the cold glass room at the top, with the sea breathing far below, she felt closer to him than anywhere else on earth.

The last ferry of the day came in under a leaden sky, and a tall stranger in a sodden coat walked up the headland to the Lighthouse Inn, carrying nothing but a single bag. He gave his name as Elias Thorne, shook the rain from his collar, and asked in a low, courteous voice whether a room might be had for the whole winter. Iris, who seldom had guests after October, looked him up and down with suspicion before she handed him a key.

That evening, in the warm and crowded kitchen, Rosa the cook ladled out a thick soup while old Abel, a retired keeper with a beard like sea foam, began a story that nobody had asked him to tell. Bosun, the inn's ancient brown dog, who regarded all visitors as a personal insult, surprised everyone by lying down on Elias's boots and refusing to move. Iris watched the two of them with narrowed eyes, unwilling to admit that the stranger was making himself at home.

Over a second bowl of soup, Elias explained, with an air of apologising for it, that he was an engineer sent by the Harbour Authority to examine the lighthouse and its machinery. Iris laid down her spoon with great care, for she had heard talk on the mainland of the old lamp being closed, and she knew that men with measuring tapes seldom brought good news. Across the table Rosa glanced at her, and in that look lay a quiet warning not to be rude to a paying guest.

Abel leaned back by the stove and, in the slow voice of a man who had told this tale many times, informed Elias that the inn had been built for the keepers' families long ago. In all that time, he said with unmistakable pride, the great light on Gull Point had never once been allowed to go dark, through storm and fog and war. Elias listened with an odd expression that Iris could not quite read, and he said nothing at all.

At midnight Iris came down to the hall to find the stranger waiting at the foot of the tower, his hands in his pockets, and she let him follow her up the stairs more out of exasperation than welcome. At the top the great lamp stood in its glass room like a sleeping animal, and beyond the windows the black sea rolled out to meet the stars. Elias stood silently for a long moment, and when he spoke, it was only to say that he had never seen anything so beautiful.

Leaning against the cold brass of the lamp, Iris told him of her father, Tom, the last keeper of Gull Point, who had taught her every secret of the machinery before he died four winters earlier. The new beacon was clever enough in calm weather, she said, but when a gale came screaming in from the north, it was the old lamp, turned by its clockwork weights, that sailors trusted. Elias listened with such gentle attention that she found herself saying more than she had intended.

The following morning Elias lay on the cold floor of the lantern room with a torch between his teeth, tracing the teeth of the gears that turned the great lamp. Deep in the mechanism, almost invisible to the naked eye, he found a hairline crack in one of the iron wheels, and he sat back on his heels with a sinking heart. Because he did not yet know what it would mean for the light, or for the woman downstairs, he decided to say nothing for the time being.

Iris took him walking along the cliff path, where the wind snatched at their coats and the winter grass was silver with frost. Far below them a colony of seals lay spread on the black rocks like heaps of wet sacking, grumbling and barking at the surf, and Elias, to his own surprise, burst out laughing. It was the first time in months that he had laughed freely, and he was dimly aware that the cause was not entirely the seals.

On the coldest night of the winter the inn's ancient boiler gave a shuddering groan and died, and the guests wrapped themselves in blankets around the kitchen stove, grumbling gently. Elias took a toolbox down to the cellar, and Iris went with him to hold the lamp, and for an hour they worked side by side in the dark among the pipes. When the first warm water rattled through the radiators, she thanked him with such sincere gratitude that he could think of nothing to say in reply.

After supper Abel brought out his battered accordion and began a slow, sweet tune from the days of his youth, and the kitchen seemed to soften around the music. Before she had time to consider it, Iris found herself being drawn across the flagstones by Elias, who danced with an awkward gravity that she found surprisingly charming. Rosa and the old dog watched from the corner with the air of spectators who knew precisely how the evening would end.

A letter arrived from Mr Dray, a senior official of the Harbour Authority, and Iris read it twice at the kitchen table with a growing coldness in her stomach. It informed her, in the careful language of officials, that the Authority would decide at the end of the winter whether the old lamp at Gull Point should be permanently retired. Beneath the signature, almost as an afterthought, was a note that the matter would be settled on the recommendation of the visiting engineer.

Iris understood at once that the man she had been dancing with held her lighthouse in his hands, and she confronted him in the yard with a face as white as the frost. She accused him of concealing his purpose, and Elias, who had never lied to her but had certainly not been forthcoming, promised that he would write an honest and fair report. They stood for a long, bitter moment staring out at the grey water, and then, almost reluctantly, they made peace.

In the evenings Elias worked in the tower, measuring and noting, and Iris began to climb the stairs with a pot of tea and sit beside him among the humming machinery. In the lamp's slow rhythm they spoke of their families, and he told her that his own father had spent most of his life at sea, rarely coming home. She told him in turn that her mother had walked out when she was small, and that the inn and the light were the only constants she had ever known.

By the fire, one evening, old Abel handed Elias a heavy, scuffed leather book with an air of deep seriousness, and explained that Tom Calloway had written in it every single night of his working life. He added, with a long look at the flames, that Tom had refused every offer to buy the inn, for he had believed with all his heart that the light belonged not to the Authority but to the sea. Elias took the book into his hands very carefully, as though the fragile pages might crumble at his touch.

Next evening Iris took the logbook down from its shelf, laid it open on the kitchen table, and showed Elias her father's upright and careful handwriting by the glow of a single candle. Each page recorded the weather, the passing ships and the hours of the lamp, and between the dry entries lay terse descriptions of storms that made her shiver. She turned the pages with tenderness, and Elias, watching her, felt a hard knot of guilt tighten inside his chest.

Elias stopped at an entry from a winter more than twenty years before, in which Tom described a ferry lost in a gale and the long night he spent turning the lamp by hand. His heart began to pound so loudly that he was sure Iris would hear it, for he knew that night better than any man alive, and he had never once spoken of it. He closed the book gently and said nothing, resolving to find the right moment and not yet daring to look for it.

At midwinter the islanders gathered at the inn for the lantern evening, a custom older than the oldest of them, and the kitchen overflowed with fishermen, farmers and children in their best coats. Elias, perched on a ladder, hung the paper lanterns along the porch one by one, and by dusk the whole building glowed against the darkness like a ship at anchor. Iris watched him from below with an expression she tried to hide, and failed.

That night the first snow began to fall, thick and silent and enormous, and Iris slipped her hand through Elias's arm as they walked up the headland towards the tower. The cliffs, the path and the dark sea had been swallowed by whiteness, and the only sound was the soft hiss of the flakes against their coats. It seemed to Iris, in that hushed and muffled world, that nothing could harm either of them.

High in the tower the great lamp turned with its familiar patient rhythm, and the beam swept across the whirling snow like a slow white hand. Iris and Elias stood close together at the glass, neither speaking, and as the church bell on the mainland rang faintly through the storm, he turned her gently towards him. At the stroke of midnight he kissed her, and for the length of that kiss the cold and the secrets and the lighthouse itself seemed to vanish.

The weeks that followed were the happiest of the winter, with long walks across the frozen headland, picnics in the lee of the rocks and evenings of cards and laughter by the kitchen fire. Bosun bounded ahead of them through the frost, barking furiously at the seals, and Iris discovered with astonishment that she laughed more now than she had in years. Even Abel, watching them from his chair, observed to Rosa that the old inn had not felt so alive since Tom's day.

At last Elias sat down to write his report, but the words refused to come, for the truth was more tangled than any official form could hold. He thought of the hairline crack in the gear, of the shrinking budget of the Authority, of the old lamp's hundred years and of the woman who climbed to it each night. Every sentence he began seemed either unfair to the lighthouse or unkind to Iris, and he tore up three drafts before dawn.

Rosa, kneading dough with furious energy at the kitchen table, told him bluntly that he must tell Iris about the night on the ferry, and that he must do it before the report was sent. Elias answered that he would do so when the report was finished and the matter was settled, since he wished to offer her good news as well as a confession. She shook the flour from her hands, gave him a long and doubtful look, and remarked that men who waited for perfect moments generally missed them.

One grey morning a black car climbed the headland, and Mr Dray stepped from it in a long dark coat, carrying a leather folder with an official air. He announced, in a smooth, reasonable voice, that the Authority intended to retire the old lamp, leave the machine beacon to do the work, and lock the tower for good. He added that the inn, which would lose much of its charm, could be bought from Iris at a most generous price.

Iris planted herself in the doorway of her own home with her arms folded and informed Mr Dray in a calm, clear voice that the Lighthouse Inn was not for sale, at any price. The official smiled politely and replied that the engineer's report would decide everything, and that he expected to receive it within the week. Behind her, in the shadows of the hall, she could feel Elias standing perfectly still.

That night, while the others slept, Iris came down to the kitchen for a glass of water and saw the draft of Elias's report lying open on the table. Her eye fell at once on a sentence at the foot of the last page, which stated in plain, cold language that the old lamp was unsafe to operate and should be shut down immediately. She read it three times, felt the floor tilt beneath her feet, and did not stop to read another word.

At first light she confronted him in the hall in a voice that shook with fury, accusing him of having come to Gull Point only to close her light and of having charmed her to make the task easier. Elias tried desperately to explain about the cracked gear, about the danger and about what he truly meant to recommend, but she was too hurt to hear a single word. She pointed to the door with a trembling finger, and her eyes were blazing and wet at once.

Elias packed his bag in complete silence, folding each shirt with the numb care of a man who cannot bear to think, while old Abel stood in the corridor and scolded Iris for her pride. She replied that she had nothing to say and that she would not be lectured in her own house, and she went to bed without wishing anyone goodnight. The inn, which had been so full of warmth and laughter, was suddenly as still as a tomb.

At dawn Elias walked down to the quay in a thin, bitter drizzle and boarded the ferry without once looking back at the headland. On the hall table at the inn he had left a thick envelope with Iris's name on it, and Rosa, finding it there, quietly slipped it into a drawer, judging that its time had not yet come. The ferry pulled away from the island, and the lighthouse shrank behind it until it was nothing but a pale finger against a pale sky.

Without him the inn felt cold and hollow, and Bosun took to sitting by the front door every evening, staring down the empty road with the patient misery of a dog who will not be persuaded. Iris threw herself into the cooking and the accounts and the entertaining of guests, but her smile was brittle, and Rosa watched her with an expression of growing impatience. Even the sea itself seemed grey and indifferent, as though it had forgotten why it had ever been worth watching.

At midnight she climbed the tower alone, as she had done for four winters before his arrival, and the old lamp turned above her with a long, grinding groan that she had never heard before. She laid her palm against the chilly brass and wondered, with a pang that was half sorrow and half shame, whether her father would have known what to do. The lamp answered only with another cry of metal, and the beam trembled as it went round.

One morning Rosa laid the thick envelope on the kitchen table and told Iris, with the severity of a woman who has said the same thing many times, that no one can afford to be proud for ever. For a long minute Iris stared at the name on the front, written in a hand she had come to know too well, and then she took it up and tore it open with fingers that were not quite steady. Rosa withdrew to the stove without another word, and the whole kitchen seemed to hold its breath until the paper came open.

Inside lay the complete pages of Elias's report, and Iris read them standing at the window in the colourless light of a winter morning, slowly at first and then with growing amazement. He recommended, in urgent language, that the old lamp be repaired rather than retired, that a new gear replace the cracked one, and that the light be kept for every sailor on that coast. The line that had so horrified her was only the first sentence of a long argument, and the rest of it read like a plea.

Clipped to the back of the report was a handwritten letter in which Elias explained that he had never intended to close the lighthouse and that he had ordered the replacement part with his own money. Iris sank into a chair and covered her face with her hands, filled with a shame so sharp that she could scarcely breathe. When it had passed, she took up a pen and wrote him a long, honest, unguarded letter of apology, and she posted it to the mainland that very afternoon.

A storm warning crackled over the radio one evening in February, and Abel, rubbing his knees with an air of grim satisfaction, declared that he could feel something savage on its way. All over the island people made ready, hauling boats up the shingle, bolting shutters and gathering lamps and blankets for what promised to be the longest night of the winter. Iris went from room to room checking the windows, and every few minutes she glanced at the dark sky with a rising dread.

At dusk the wind rose to a scream, and a tremendous crack from the direction of the cliffs told the island that a power line had come down. The machine beacon on Gull Point flickered, died, and left the whole of Harrow Bay, from the headland to the distant coast, lying in a blackness so complete that it seemed to have weight. In the kitchen no one spoke, for everyone understood that the light which sailors trusted had been taken from them.

Over the crackling radio, Captain Quill of the ferry Kittiwake reported in a voice stretched thin by fear that she was lost in the bay, with passengers aboard and the rocks close ahead. Iris stood motionless with her hand over her mouth, for she knew that stretch of water, and she knew precisely how many ships had died on those rocks in the days before the lamp. Then Iris seized her coat, and Abel seized his, and together they ran out into the screaming dark towards the tower.

They flung themselves up the tower stairs and into the lantern room, where the great lamp stood dark and silent, its cracked gear jammed fast against the wheel. Abel looked at Iris, and Iris looked at the heavy iron crank hanging from its hook on the wall, and without a word they took it down together. If the light was to turn that night, it would have to be turned by hand, through the long hours of the gale, until the ship was safe.

One by one the islanders climbed the stairs, the fishermen and farmers and tired mothers, and each took a turn at the iron handle until their arms burned and passed it to the next. Rosa came up with soup and tea in great steaming cans, Bosun lay across the top step like a guard, and the beam swept steadily across the roaring water with a rhythm that never once faltered. Hour after hour the great lamp turned, and hour after hour the people of the island kept their promise to the dark.

On the pitching deck of the ferry, soaked to the bone and wedged against a rail, Elias clutched the heavy parcel containing the new gear and peered into the blackness through the spray. He had come back because of her letter and because he could not stay away, and beside him, grey with seasickness, sat Mr Dray, whom he had at last persuaded to see the old light with his own eyes. Suddenly a pale beam swept across the waves, and Elias remembered, with a wrench that nearly stopped his breath, a frightened boy of ten who had watched that same light from a boat very like this one.

Captain Quill steered by the beam alone, counting the seconds between each sweep, and threaded the shuddering ferry between the black teeth of the rocks with the skill of a woman who had spent her life on that water. No one on board spoke, and many of them were praying, until at last, in the first grey streaks of dawn, the dark shape of the harbour wall rose from the sea ahead. A ragged cheer went up from the passengers, and the Kittiwake slid into the shelter of the quay like a tired animal coming home.

The whole village had gathered on the quay to watch the ferry's ropes go ashore, and a tremendous roar greeted the first passengers as they stumbled down the gangway. Mr Dray came last, white-faced and silent, with his fine coat torn and his hat gone, and he stood for a long time looking up at the headland, where a pale beam still turned. Nobody could find anything to say to him, and for once he did not appear to expect it.

Elias seized the parcel, pushed through the crowd, and began to run, up the steep path along the cliff and through the thin grey light, with the wind screaming at his back. His lungs burned and his legs shook with exhaustion, but he did not slow his pace until the tower door loomed before him at the top of the path. There, at the threshold, with her coat hanging off her shoulders, stood the woman he had left behind.

Iris's face was grey with the long night, and her hands were blistered from the crank, and for a moment neither of them could speak. Then they both said sorry at once, and Elias told her in a rush that he had been the boy in her father's logbook, the child whom the light had saved. She took his hand, drew him up the tower stairs, and showed him the page where her father had written of that night, and they wept together.

Mr Dray climbed slowly up the cliff behind them, entered the lantern room with the air of a man entering a church, and removed what remained of his hat. He told them in a low, shaken voice that he had been on that ferry, and that he would never sign anything to put the old light out. Standing there with his thin hair blown wild by the wind, he looked for the first time like a human being rather than an official.

Within the week the Harbour Authority met in emergency session and agreed to fund the full repair of the old lamp, to retain the machine beacon only as a second light, and to declare the tower a heritage lighthouse. The Lighthouse Inn would become the keepers' lodge, with Iris Calloway as its keeper, and the islanders who had turned the crank all night would be remembered in a plaque by the door. Iris read the letter three times, and then she laughed, and then she cried, and then she went to find Elias.

When spring arrived, with primroses along the cliff path and the sea turning from grey to a hopeful green, Elias fitted the new gear into the old lamp, while Iris held the lantern steady beside him. They closed the casing, stood back, and let the great weights fall, and the lamp began to turn with a smooth, silent, steady rhythm like the beating of a patient heart. Neither of them spoke, for there was nothing that could have been said better than the soft sweep of that light across the water.

One midnight in the tower, as the lamp turned above them and the sea murmured below, Elias drew a small ring from his pocket and knelt on the cold floor beside the great brass wheel. He asked Iris to marry him in a voice that was not entirely steady, and she said yes before he had even finished the question. The beam swept out across the dark water as though the whole coast were applauding, and Bosun, who had followed them up the stairs, thumped his tail against the boards.

In the high summer they were married on the cliff with the sea shining below them and the whole island gathered in its best clothes, the fishermen scrubbed and the children carrying flowers. Abel played the accordion until the stars came out, Rosa's enormous cake was eaten to the last crumb, and Bosun, entrusted with the rings in a small box tied to his collar, behaved with perfect dignity. Captain Quill sounded the Kittiwake's horn across the bay as the couple kissed, and the echo rolled out over the water.

A year later, at the stroke of midnight, Iris and Elias climbed the spiral stairs together with a lantern swinging between them, as they had on a hundred nights before. At the top the great lamp turned smoothly in its glass room, and out on the dark water a ship passed safely beneath the sweeping beam, her crew never knowing the story of the light that guided them. Iris leaned against her husband's shoulder, looked out at the sea her father had loved, and knew that she was home.
